The question of whether remote work is more productive than office work is genuinely contested, with credible research on both sides. Several studies cited in d1 (University of Chicago, Harvard, Stanford) found remote work productivity was over 7% higher than in-office productivity on average, and Stanford researchers found remote workers 9% more efficient than office-based ones by summer 2022. Similarly, d4 reports that remote workers are 35–40% more productive than in-office counterparts, and d3 (PwC) found 52% of executives said employee productivity improved under remote work. Gallup research in d6 also concludes that remote workers offer leaders the greatest gains in business outcomes through higher engagement and productivity.

However, opposing evidence is equally substantial. A Stanford working paper cited in d11 found that fully remote work is associated with 10% to 20% lower productivity than fully in-person work, with communication challenges and lack of motivation as key factors. d2 (Chicago Booth) cites a Rutgers researcher who states "Working at home is always less productive than working at the office. Always," with a calibrated model showing the average high-skill worker is less productive at home even post-pandemic. d8 (Washington Post) argues that permanent remote work would make workers less productive over the medium to long term due to lost face-to-face learning and innovation benefits. d10 (The Economist) adds that recent research found feedback between colleagues dropped sharply after moving to remote work and that office workers picked up skills more quickly than remote workers.

In summary, the research is genuinely divided: some studies show remote work boosts productivity, particularly for individual task completion and short-term output [d1, d3, d4, d6], while others find it reduces productivity over the longer term due to weaker collaboration, mentoring, and skill development [d2, d8, d10, d11]. The answer likely depends on the type of work, the degree of remoteness (fully remote vs. hybrid), and the time horizon considered [d9, d11].
